intro: Looking for a chancery barrister near you usually means a dispute over property, a will or inheritance, a trust, or a company or insolvency matter has become serious enough to need specialist help. Chancery work often involves complex documents and careful analysis, and it can feel daunting to know where to start. We can introduce you to a suitable UK barrister who will quote you directly, with fees on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a chancery barrister usually need
need_lead: Most people searching this way are facing a dispute or a difficult legal question that sits within chancery work and want to speak to someone who handles it regularly.
needs: You are in a dispute over the ownership of property or land and need advice on your position before deciding what to do next.
A will or inheritance is being contested, or you are unsure whether an estate has been dealt with properly, and you want specialist guidance.
There is a disagreement about a trust, who the trustees are or how the assets should be managed.
Your company is involved in a dispute with a business partner, shareholder or director and you need clear advice on the options.
You are dealing with insolvency, a creditor is pursuing you, or a company you are connected with is in financial difficulty.
context_heading: Understanding chancery barristers and how to instruct one
context: Chancery barristers specialise in property, trusts, wills and estates, company and insolvency disputes. Barristers in England and Wales are regulated by the Bar Standards Board (BSB), and you can check the Barristers' Register to see whether someone holds a current practising certificate and whether they are authorised to accept instructions directly from the public. In Scotland the equivalent professionals are advocates, regulated through the Faculty of Advocates.

Barristers usually work from chambers, with clerks who manage diaries and fees. Many barristers can be instructed through a solicitor in the traditional way, and those registered under the Public Access scheme can be instructed directly by members of the public for suitable matters. Because chancery work often involves complex documents, it helps to have your paperwork organised before you speak to anyone.
tell_heading: What to tell us when you enquire
tell: Describe the type of dispute in a sentence or two, such as a property disagreement, an inheritance dispute, a trust issue or a company matter.
Explain where you are in the process, for example whether court proceedings have started or you are still considering your options.
Say whether a solicitor is already involved, since this affects how a barrister can be instructed.
Mention the key documents you hold, such as a will, a trust deed, a contract or correspondence with the other side.
Give your location and say how far you are able to travel, since you searched for a chancery barrister near you.
Set out what you are hoping to achieve, whether that is advice, help with mediation or representation in a hearing.
questions: Are you authorised to accept instructions directly from the public under the Public Access scheme?
Do you handle the particular type of chancery dispute I am facing?
How do you usually work with clients on a matter like mine, and will I deal with you or with your clerks?
What information and documents would you like from me before we begin?
How will your fees be calculated, and can you give me an estimate of the likely cost?
Would mediation be suitable for my situation, or is a court hearing more likely?

faqs.q: What kinds of matters does a chancery barrister deal with?
faqs.a: Chancery barristers specialise in property, trusts, wills and estates, company and insolvency disputes. Inheritance disputes are common, and much of the work involves complex documents. If your matter fits one of these areas, a chancery barrister may be the right person to speak to.

faqs.q: Can I instruct a chancery barrister directly, without a solicitor?
faqs.a: Some barristers are registered under the Public Access scheme and can be instructed directly by members of the public for suitable matters. Others are usually instructed through a solicitor in the traditional way. You can check the Barristers' Register to see whether someone is authorised to accept direct instructions.

faqs.q: How do I check that a barrister is properly regulated?
faqs.a: Barristers in England and Wales are regulated by the Bar Standards Board (BSB). The Barristers' Register shows whether someone holds a current practising certificate and whether they are authorised to accept instructions directly from the public. In Scotland the equivalent professionals are advocates, regulated through the Faculty of Advocates.

faqs.q: Will mediation help with my chancery dispute?
faqs.a: Mediation can resolve many cases, and it is often worth asking a barrister whether it suits your situation before assuming a court hearing is the only route. A barrister can advise on the options that fit the particular dispute. The right approach depends on the documents and on what the other side is willing to do.
